title: Contrasting Warming Responses of Crops Harvested for Aboveground and Belowground Organs: A Global‐Meta Analysis
content:
Global warming exacerbates heat stress and threatens food production, but its effects vary by crop type and harvested organ. Our results reveal that warming causes larger yield reductions in crops harvested for aboveground organs (CA) compared to those harvested for belowground organs (CB). Yield losses are primarily driven by declines in the number of end-products, with short-day CA crops being most vulnerable, followed by stem tuber CB crops. Root tuber CB crops are least affected. Latitude further modulates these effects: warming at higher latitudes amplifies losses in long-day CA crops but mitigates or reverses impacts in short-day CA and root tuber CB crops. These findings highlight that warming effects on yield are organ-, crop type-, and latitude-specific, and suggest that adaptive strategies, such as adjusting sowing dates or relocating short-day crops to higher latitudes, could mitigate warming-induced yield losses.


ABSTRACT

Global warming intensifies heat stress and threatens global food production, but the extent of yield loss varies with crop type and harvested organ. To disentangle these patterns, we conducted a meta-analysis of 96 studies comparing warming responses in crops harvested for aboveground organs (CA) versus belowground organs (CB). Warming resulted in larger yield reductions in CA than in CB crops, with end-product number being more sensitive to warming stress than end-product mass in both crop types. Among crop groups, short-day CA crops experienced the greatest warming-induced yield loss, followed by stem tuber CB crops, whereas root tuber CB crops were least affected. Latitudinal gradients further modulated responses: warming at higher latitudes exacerbated losses in long-day CA crops but alleviated or reversed impacts in short-day CA and root tuber CB crops. These findings demonstrate that warming effects are organ-, crop type-, and latitude-dependent, rather than uniform across agricultural systems. By synthesizing diverse experimental evidence, this study provides a quantitative framework for understanding crop-specific vulnerabilities to heat stress, offering new insights for breeding heat-tolerant varieties and guiding adaptive management under climate change.
